intro: Something, nothing, someone, nobody, somewhere, nowhere, everyone… English builds these words with some-, any-, no- and every-, with the same rules as some and any (lesson 31). You need them in everyday conversation.
objectifs: Build and understand the words with some-, any-, no-, every- (+ thing, one / body, where).
Choose between some- (positive, offers), any- (negatives, questions) and no- (negative meaning with a positive verb).
Avoid double negatives: I don't know anything / I know nothing, never “I don't know nothing”.
Put an adjective or “else” after these words (something nice, someone else) and use a singular verb.

texte: Combine some-, any-, no-, every- with -thing (a thing), -one or -body (a person) and -where (a place). “-one” and “-body” mean exactly the same; “-body” is a little more informal.
“No one” is two words (sometimes “no-one” in British English). The others are one word: someone, anybody, nothing, everywhere.

Use “some-” in positive sentences: There's someone at the door. I want to eat something. Also use it in questions when you offer or ask for something and expect “yes”: Would you like something to drink? Can someone help me?
Use “any-” in negative sentences (with not / n't) and in most questions: I can't see anything. Is anyone there? Did you go anywhere at the weekend?
exemples: Would you like something to eat?
I don't know anyone in this city.
Is there anything in the fridge?

texte: “Nothing, no one, nobody, nowhere” already have a negative meaning. So the verb stays POSITIVE: I know nothing. Nobody called. Never say “I don't know nothing”: in standard English, two negatives are wrong.

So there are two ways to say the same thing: I can't see anything (more common in speaking) / I can see nothing (stronger, more written). As the subject of a sentence, only no- is possible: Nobody knows (never “Anybody doesn't know”).
“Nothing / nobody” can also be short answers: What's in the box? — Nothing. Who's there? — No one.

sections.titre: Any- in positive sentences: “it doesn't matter which”
texte: In a positive sentence, “any-” means “it doesn't matter which thing / person / place”: You can sit anywhere. Anyone can learn English.
“Every-” means “all”: everything, everyone, everywhere. Be careful: everyone / everybody takes a SINGULAR verb, even if the meaning is plural: Everyone is here.
exemples: At any time (anytime: mostly US; UK: any time).
I'll eat anything. I'm so hungry!

sections.titre: Adjectives, else, and the pronouns after
texte: The adjective goes AFTER these words, not before: something interesting, nothing new, somewhere warm. No “of”: don't say “something of interesting”.
“Else” means “other” or “more”, and also goes after: someone else, anything else?, everywhere else.
You can add “to + verb”: something to eat, nothing to do, somewhere to sleep.
To refer back to “someone, anyone, everyone”, people often use they / their: Someone left their umbrella. Is everyone ready? Have they got their tickets?
exemples: Did you do anything special at the weekend?
There's nothing to do in this village.

formule: some- (positive, offers) · any- (negatives, questions; “it doesn't matter which” in positives) · no- + positive verb · every- + singular verb · something + adjective / else / to + verb
prononciation: “nothing” /ˈnʌθɪŋ/: the o sounds like /ʌ/ as in “mother”, not like “no”. But “nobody” /ˈnəʊbədi/ starts like “no”.
The /θ/ in -thing: tongue between the teeth. Don't say “somesing” or “someting”.
erreurs: I don't know anything. / I know nothing.
There isn't anybody at home. / There's nobody at home.
I didn't go anywhere. / I went nowhere.

dialogue.contexte: Two colleagues arrive for a meeting at a company's offices in Lausanne.
lignes: Hello? Is anyone here? The room is empty.
No, nobody's here. Maybe the meeting is somewhere else.
Did someone send an email about it?
Let me check… No, there's nothing in my inbox.
Look, there's something on the table. It's a note.
It says: “Everyone is in room 4B. Coffee for everybody!”
Great! I didn't have anything for breakfast.
Me neither. Let's go. I hope there's something to eat too!

mots: I've got something to tell you.
a thing that you don't name exactly
I want to live somewhere warm.
in or to a place you don't name
not in or to any place
I looked everywhere for my keys.

exercices.consigne: Complete with something, anything, someone or anyone.
items: I didn't buy ___ at the market.
I want to tell you ___ important.
I can't hear ___. It's very quiet.

exercices.consigne: Rewrite the sentence with nothing, nobody or nowhere (same meaning).
items: I don't have anything to say.
I have nothing to say. / I've got nothing to say.
There isn't anyone in the office.
There's nobody in the office. / There's no one in the office.
We didn't go anywhere last summer.
She doesn't know anything about it.
___ is ready. Let's start! (all the people)
I want to watch something ___. (it makes you laugh)
I looked ___ for my glasses. (in all places)

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Correct it.
items: I didn't see anybody. / I saw nobody.
Is there something of interesting on TV?
Is there anything interesting on TV?
Nobody likes him. / No one likes him.

exercices.consigne: Write one sentence for each idea, with a word from the lesson.
items: Nobody is perfect. / No one is perfect.
It doesn't matter which seat you take.
There's nothing to eat. / There isn't anything to eat.
You want to travel to a sunny place (you don't know which one).
I'd like to go somewhere sunny.

exercices.consigne: Write five sentences about your weekend or your week with at least five different words from the lesson (one with no- and one with else or an adjective).
items: On Saturday I didn't go anywhere. I stayed at home and did nothing special. In the evening, someone from my family called me. On Sunday we went somewhere new: a small restaurant by the river. Everyone loved it.

a_retenir: some- (positive, offers), any- (negatives, questions), no- (positive verb), every- (all).
No double negatives: I don't know anything / I know nothing.
Negative subject: Nobody knows, Nothing happened.
Adjective, else or to + verb after: something new, someone else, nothing to do.
everyone / everybody + singular verb; refer back with they / their.
